title: Complex trigonometric functions and equations
terms: complex sine; complex cosine; complex tangent; complex cotangent; complex secant; complex cosecant; trigonometric identities over C.

Define cos z = (e + e )/2 and sin z = (e − e )/(2i). Quotients define tangent, cotangent,

secant, and cosecant where their denominators are nonzero. Addition formulas, sin z + cos z = 1,
and period 2π remain valid over C.
Unlike their restrictions to the real axis, complex sine and cosine are unbounded. To solve equa-

tions such as cos z = a, put w = e , solve a quadratic for nonzero w, then use all logarithms of
w. Keeping all periods is essential to obtain the full solution set.
Explicitly, tan z = sin z/ cos z, cot z = cos z/sin z, sec z = 1/ cos z, and csc z = 1/ sin z, wherever

the indicated denominator is nonzero. Thus sec z − tan z = 1 and csc z − cot z = 1 on
their respective domains. Each identity may extend across points where its separate terms are
undefined, if their difference has a removable singularity.

question.text:
How many complex solutions does tan z = i have?
(A) None.
(B) Exactly one.
(C) Exactly two.
(D) Countably infinitely many.
(E) Uncountably infinitely many.

1)/(i(w + 1)), with w ̸= −1. Equating this to i gives w − 1 = −(w + 1) and hence
w = 0, impossible for an exponential. Thus complex tangent can omit a value even though
complex sine and cosine are unbounded.

question.text:
Where is the complex function tan z singular?
(A) At z = kπi, with simple poles
(B) Nowhere in C
(C) At z = π/2 + kπ, with simple poles
(D) At z = kπ, with simple poles
(E) At z = π/2 + kπ, with removable singularities

solution.text:
The zeros of cos z are π/2 + kπ. Its derivative − sin z is nonzero there, while the numerator
sin z is also nonzero. Thus each is a simple pole of the quotient.

Initially define F (z) = sec z − tan z where cos z ̸= 0 and G(z) = csc z − cot z where sin z ̸= 0.
Which statement is correct?
(A) Both functions extend to the constant function one on all of C.
(B) Only F has any removable singularities.
(C) Only G extends to an entire function.
(D) Both have nonremovable poles at their excluded points.
(E) Both extend to the constant function zero.

solution.text:
2 2 2 2
On their domains, F = (1 − sin z)/ cos z = 1 and G = (1 − cos z)/ sin z = 1. Thus each
omitted point can be filled with value one to give a holomorphic function everywhere. Poles
in individual summands can cancel exactly in a difference.
